title: El Niño and a Warming World: What Leaders Need to Know
gist: A World Economic Forum Agenda Dialogues session billing sheet argues that El Niño events are becoming more economically consequential as global temperatures rise, with transmission channels running through extreme weather, food and water security, and supply chains. Speakers are WEF's Akanksha Khatri and World Meteorological Organization Secretary-General Celeste Saulo; the page is a promotional blurb, not a transcript, so no data or arguments are actually presented.

insights.claim: El Niño events are described as becoming increasingly consequential for economies, ecosystems and societies as global temperatures continue to rise, implying the baseline warming trend amplifies the impact of an already-recurring climate oscillation rather than acting independently of it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Treat El Niño years as a rising-amplitude macro variable rather than a repeatable historical analogue; prior-cycle playbooks for soft commodities, insurance losses and emerging-market inflation may understate the tail.
insights.quote: As global temperatures continue to rise, El Niño events are becoming increasingly consequential for economies, ecosystems and societies.
insights.locator: As global temperatures continue to rise

insights.claim: The framing positions the current period as 'an era of growing climate volatility', treating volatility rather than a single directional shift as the operative planning variable for leaders.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Volatility framing favors option-like exposures — weather derivatives, reinsurance pricing power, resilience capex — over simple directional climate trades.
insights.quote: an era of growing climate volatility
insights.locator: the decisions needed to build resilience

insights.claim: The stated impact channels of El Niño in a warming world are extreme weather, food and water security, and supply chains — a chain that runs from a physical climate signal to corporate input costs and logistics rather than only to environmental outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete watchlist for the next event: agricultural commodities, water-intensive industrials and mining, and freight/logistics chokepoints exposed to drought or flooding.
insights.quote: from its impacts on extreme weather, food and water security, and supply chains to the decisions needed to build resilience
insights.locator: This session will explore what leaders need to understand

insights.claim: The agenda is pitched around 'decisions needed to build resilience', framing the response as capital allocation and preparation by corporate and political leaders rather than as emissions mitigation.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals institutional attention shifting from decarbonization narratives toward adaptation and resilience spending — a different investable set (infrastructure, water, insurance, forecasting/data).
insights.locator: the decisions needed to build resilience

insights.claim: The session pairs the World Meteorological Organization's Secretary-General, Celeste Saulo, with Akanksha Khatri, Head of Strategic Insight & Impact and an Executive Committee member at the World Economic Forum, putting an official meteorological authority directly into a business-leadership forum.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Official WMO seasonal outlooks are becoming an input channel into corporate planning circles; watch WMO El Niño/La Niña updates as a leading indicator that boardrooms are now primed to act on.

insights.claim: The full video session is gated to World Economic Forum partners and digital members, with only the audio released publicly — meaning the substantive content behind this listing is not in the public text.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Low standalone information value; the page is a pointer, so any real signal requires the gated session rather than this summary.
